To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the cell surface of living cells is permeable to all ions of strong electrolyte solutions and to all other substances, and that it is not possible to measure permeability in the generally accepted meaning of the term, because of the large activity of the cell surface, which is responsible for the large differences in ionic concentration between cell and surrounding fluid, and also for the fact that the cell surface can be made permeable for any substance, even those of large molecular size, by suitable treatment.
the active transport of sodium ions outwards and of potassium ions inwards is the main factor responsible for the differences in concentration of these ions between cells and surrounding fluids.

the cell surface, when it is active and not passive, is a selective membrane, that is to say it is permeable to some ions but not to others, and that the selectivity is such that it will allow the passage of ions of opposite sign but of equal valency.

the ion transport across living membranes, whether cell surfaces or other membranes, is a complex phenomenon, and cannot be understood in terms of the simple diffusion theory of permeability, as has been done in many cases in the past.
